sources.title: Landscaping for wildlife with native plants
Planting and establishing trees and shrubs

fit.requires: Confirm permitted ground space, plants and establishment care.

guide.title: Plant a native pollinator space
guide.description: Turn a patch of your yard into a planted space, with a care plan you can keep.
guide.purpose: Provide locally suitable flowers and habitat. Start small enough to maintain; HALO does not estimate pollinator or farm benefits.
guide.effort: A site check, planting day and ongoing care
guide.cost: Plants, tools and mulch vary locally. No price estimate is loaded.
guide.scope: North Carolina guidance. Recheck species and growing conditions elsewhere.
guide.suitability: A permitted yard or shared garden. A container is an alternative for flowers, not a substitute for a tree planting site.
materials: Site sketch and measuring tape
Locally suitable native plants with labels
Gloves, hand trowel or shovel
Watering can or hose and organic mulch
constraints: Get the owner’s permission and locate buried utilities before digging.
Check mature plant size, local rules and access. Do not disturb established tree roots.
Have a reachable water source and someone able to maintain the planting.

steps.title: Check the space and get permission
instructions: Sketch the planting area. Note sunlight in the morning, midday and late afternoon, drainage, and available space.
Confirm permission and utility-marking requirements before excavation. Choose a smaller accessible area if digging or ongoing care is difficult.
steps.checkpoint: Record the permitted area, observed conditions and who will maintain it.

steps.title: Choose native plants for this site
instructions: Match plants to your observed light, moisture and mature size using the linked Extension guidance.
Aim for flowers across spring, summer and fall. Eastern redbud, cardinal flower and goldenrod are examples to investigate, not automatic recommendations for your site.
Sketch spacing at mature size and retain plant names and nursery instructions.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a plant list with its site requirements before buying or digging.

steps.title: Plant without burying the crown
instructions: For a small container-grown tree or shrub, measure the root ball. Dig only that deep and make the hole two to three times wider; roughen slick sides.
Handle the plant by its root ball. Ask the nursery about circling roots. Position the trunk flare at or slightly above the surrounding ground.
Backfill with the removed soil, water it in and finish level with surrounding ground. Add 2 to 3 inches of organic mulch, keeping it at least 6 inches from the trunk.
For flowers, follow their planting-depth instructions rather than applying the tree dimensions.
steps.checkpoint: Record the species, planting date and number planted. A photo is optional, not proof of a benefit.

steps.title: Keep a care and seasonal check
instructions: Check root-ball moisture during establishment; adjust watering to rain and site conditions instead of a fixed app schedule.
Keep mulch away from stems. Note survival, bloom timing and weeds, and ask Extension about problems you cannot identify.
Choose your own check-back date and record what needs replacing or adjusting.
steps.checkpoint: Save a care plan and one factual follow-up observation.

guide.completion: A permitted site was planted, plant names and date were recorded, and a care check was chosen. A plan alone can remain paused instead of being marked planted.
guide.followup: Review establishment and bloom gaps later. Record survival or observed visitors without turning them into a measured biodiversity increase.

Bee hotel design, placement and maintenance

fit.requires: Adult tool supervision, suitable mounting and seasonal nest maintenance are required.

guide.title: Make a small solitary-bee house
guide.description: Build or assemble a modest nesting shelter, then take responsibility for its maintenance.
guide.purpose: Offer nesting space for cavity-nesting bees. A hotel is not a honeybee hive or a guaranteed conservation benefit.
guide.cost: Use a suitable existing shelter or price untreated wood and nesting materials locally.
guide.scope: NC State guidance for North Carolina. Species and seasonal timing differ elsewhere.
guide.suitability: A permitted garden with flowers and a sheltered mounting point. Choose habitat planting instead if you cannot maintain nests.
materials: Small wooden housing and mounting hardware, or the cut list below
Natural reeds or plant stems, smooth and closed at one end
Ruler, saw, drill, clamps, wood glue and 23 #8 × 1¼-inch trim screws for the source build
Opaque emergence box with protected exit holes for later maintenance
constraints: Adults handle cutting, drilling and secure mounting. Avoid entrances where people must brush past nests.
Do not purchase or release bees. Never open, clean or discard occupied nests.
Do not use plastic or glass tubes, exposed paper straw bundles, pinecones or moss as nesting material.

steps.title: Choose a maintainable design
instructions: Keep the shelter small, with fewer than 100 tunnels. Check that you can remove and replace nesting materials later.
For a wooden build, use the linked measured shelter plan with an experienced adult. It includes its cut list, roof assembly and mounting directions.
Prepare an emergence box before installing nests, so used tubes can be retired without trapping residents.
steps.checkpoint: Choose a build or assembly method and name the person responsible for upkeep.

steps.title: Prepare breathable nesting tubes
instructions: Use natural reeds or stems with one closed end and smooth, splinter-free entrances.
Use varied diameters from about 2 to 12.7 mm; lengths around 6 inches, or 3 to 8 inches, suit the Extension guide. Do not treat one diameter as suitable for every bee.
Keep tubes secured inside the shelter. Paper liners belong inside sturdy wooden tunnels, not as loose exposed bundles.
steps.checkpoint: Record tube material, lengths and approximate tunnel count.

steps.title: Mount a sheltered, stable house
instructions: Protect the entrances with a roof overhang of a couple of inches and provide drainage in the shelter floor.
Mount about 5 feet above ground where observation is easy and vegetation cannot block entrances. Follow mounting-hardware instructions.
Consider morning sun, afternoon shade and prevailing wind; southeast is a common starting orientation, not a universal rule. Keep nearby flowers available.
steps.checkpoint: Record the location, mounting check and sunlight you actually observe.

steps.title: Observe and renew responsibly
instructions: During active nesting, leave tubes and entrances in place. Observe from a distance without opening nests.
In fall or winter, follow the source to move intact occupied tubes into an opaque emergence box. Keep it cold and protected, not in a heated home.
If stored in an unheated shed, bring the box outdoors after the last spring frost so emerging insects can leave. Restock the main house with fresh tubes.
Keep used tubes in the emergence box for a full growing season before retiring them. Follow the source to ensure residents have left rather than guessing emptiness.
steps.checkpoint: Keep an observation and a seasonal maintenance plan, even if no nests are used.

guide.completion: A stable shelter was installed and a responsible emergence-box and maintenance plan was recorded. No occupancy is required to honestly record assembly.
guide.followup: Check shelter condition and later seasonal maintenance. A capped tube is an observation, not a species identification or a count of bees saved.

sources.title: Build a solar oven design challenge (PDF)

fit.requires: A permitted sunny test space, a suitable thermometer and adult supervision are required.

guide.title: Build a solar-energy experiment
guide.description: Make a simple solar oven, measure temperature and improve one part of your design.
guide.purpose: Explore how sunlight can be collected and converted to heat. This is a learning experiment, not a food-safety or energy-savings claim.
guide.effort: One supervised build and a sunny-day test
guide.cost: Reuse clean materials where practical. A suitable thermometer may need to be borrowed or purchased.
guide.scope: Adapted from NASA’s classroom design challenge. Outdoor results depend on conditions.
guide.suitability: A sunny permitted space, an adult supervising tools and heating, and a thermometer suitable for the experiment.
materials: Clean cardboard box at least 40 cm wide, foil and black construction paper
Transparent plastic wrap, tape and an aluminum pie pan
Thermometer, timer and a sheet for recording time and temperature
Adult-handled cutting tools and heat protection
constraints: Use this version without food. It cannot establish whether food can be eaten or water is disinfected.
An adult handles tools and hot surfaces. Stay with the experiment and let parts cool before touching.
Do not stare at the Sun or direct reflected light toward eyes, roads or flammable materials.

steps.title: Draw a testable design
instructions: Sketch a box with a dark absorbing surface, foil to redirect light and a transparent cover to retain heat.
Choose where the thermometer will sit and how you will read it consistently. Use a stable sunny spot and plan one design change to compare later.
steps.checkpoint: Keep your sketch and write what you predict will happen.

steps.title: Assemble the oven in order
instructions: Line the interior sides with foil. Lay black paper on the box floor and put the empty pan and thermometer inside before adding the transparent cover.
Tape the cover securely while keeping the thermometer readable. Stabilize any reflector so it cannot blow or shine toward people.
Check the whole assembly with the supervising adult before placing it in sun. Stop if materials soften or scorch.
steps.checkpoint: Record the materials and thermometer placement you used.

steps.title: Measure rather than guess
instructions: Record the initial temperature and time, then read again after 5 minutes. Note units, sunlight, clouds and any movement.
NASA’s challenge uses a 5°C rise in 5 minutes as a design target, not a promised result. Keep your actual result even when the oven does not warm.
Do not add invented readings or translate temperature change into household energy savings.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the starting and ending readings, units, elapsed time and conditions.

steps.title: Change one thing and repeat
instructions: Let the setup cool. Choose one change, such as reflector position or the absorbing surface, and explain why.
Repeat the same timed test as closely as conditions allow. Note differences in sun or weather that limit comparison.
Compare your actual readings and describe what you learned. Reuse or dispose of materials responsibly.
steps.checkpoint: Record the changed design, a second test and one limitation of the comparison.

guide.completion: The oven was built, real temperatures were recorded and a design change was tested or explained as not feasible. A temperature target need not be met.
guide.followup: Choose another controlled comparison if useful. This teaches an energy concept but does not demonstrate a household emission reduction.

guide.title: Get to know your water
guide.description: Get a dated source, ask a specific question and carry the answer into your home records.
guide.purpose: Resolve a practical water-information question without treating a public system sample as a test of your own tap.
guide.effort: Three short sessions, at your pace
guide.cost: Reading public information has no app fee. Ask a certified lab for any testing quote.
guide.scope: US public-system reports and private-well resources; local testing needs vary.
guide.suitability: Renters, owners and private-water households. No sampling equipment is needed for this information project.
materials: Your specific question
Water provider name or known private-well context
A dated public report or your own existing lab result
A place to keep the source and reply
constraints: Use a certified laboratory’s own collection instructions for testing.
Do not infer contamination, or its absence, from appearance, a missing value or a map pattern.
A reply or checklist does not replace a home measurement.

steps.title: Write down what you want to understand about your water.
instructions: Write one answerable question, such as which dated report applies to your provider or which certified lab can address your testing concern.
Record whether the question is about a public water system or a private well. Leave an uncertain provider name uncertain.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a question and the known water context, without guessing a result.

steps.title: Review a dated source or the test records you already have.
instructions: For a public supply, use EPA’s report finder or the provider’s official site. Keep the report year, provider name and link.
For an existing lab result, keep the sample date, matrix, units and qualifications. A utility report and a tap sample have different scopes.
steps.checkpoint: Record one dated source and what it can actually tell you.

steps.title: Choose a provider, lab or public resource to ask.
instructions: Ask the water provider about its report. For a private well, contact the local health department or a state-certified drinking-water laboratory.
Ask which tests or records address the question, what the costs are and whose sampling instructions must be followed. Do not collect a sample before obtaining the lab’s instructions.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the contact route and your prepared question. Opening a website is not a reply.

steps.title: Record what you learned and choose a follow-up.
instructions: Record the answer and its date, or note that you are waiting. Preserve the original question and source.
If you choose testing, continue into Homeguard to record actual arrangements and results. Deliberately save a follow-up in My Week rather than treating the reply date as a due date.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the answer, remaining uncertainty and a next step you chose.

guide.completion: A source was reviewed, the question was resolved or its remaining limits recorded, and a deliberate follow-up was chosen.
guide.followup: Review the response, source date or a new home test when available. No score changes merely because the project is completed.

fit.requires: Confirm permission, container placement and load limits.

guide.title: Grow a balcony pollinator garden
guide.description: Choose plants for a small outdoor space and give them a manageable care routine.
guide.purpose: Create a locally suitable planted container habitat without requiring a private yard.
guide.effort: A space check, planting and ongoing care
guide.cost: Containers, plants and potting mix vary locally. Reuse suitable containers if they drain properly.
guide.scope: US balcony guidance. Local plant selection and building rules still apply.
guide.suitability: A permitted balcony, patio or outdoor ledge with a suitable load limit and secure container placement.
materials: Measured outdoor space and sunlight notes
Locally suitable plants with their mature dimensions
Stable containers with drainage and potting mix
Gloves, hand trowel and watering can
constraints: Confirm building permission, balcony load limits and secure placement before adding containers.
Do not attach planters to a railing or obstruct exits without permission and appropriate hardware.
Choose plants and container size for the actual site. A region alone does not establish suitability.

steps.title: Measure your space and watch the light
instructions: Confirm permission and a stable location away from doors and edges. Ask the building manager about load limits if they are not known.
Measure the usable area and note actual sun and shade at different times. Leave clear room to move around them.
steps.checkpoint: Keep dimensions, permission and observed light.

steps.title: Choose a small, local plant mix
instructions: Use the source’s regional plant resources and local Extension advice to select plants for that light and container space.
Compare mature height, width and bloom times before buying. Start with a few plants that you can water and maintain.
steps.checkpoint: Record plant names and their container/site requirements.

steps.title: Plant and arrange stable containers
instructions: Use containers with drainage holes and a suitable potting mix. Follow each plant’s depth and container instructions.
Water after planting and arrange plants so none can fall or obstruct access. Do not assume runoff can drain onto another balcony.
steps.checkpoint: Record plants installed and the care instructions you retained.

steps.title: Keep an establishment check
instructions: Check moisture and plant condition regularly; containers can dry faster than ground soil.
Keep an observation of survival or flowering and choose a care check. No pollinator-count or health benefit is inferred.
steps.checkpoint: Choose a care date and record one factual plant observation.

guide.completion: Permitted containers were planted and a realistic care check was chosen.
guide.followup: Adjust the care routine to actual plant condition and seasonal requirements.

fit.requires: Confirm mature root and canopy space, utilities, permission and establishment care.

guide.title: Plant and establish one native tree
guide.description: Give one suitable tree the space and early care it needs.
guide.purpose: Establish a locally appropriate tree as a long-term habitat project, not a quantified carbon offset.
guide.effort: Site planning, planting and establishment care
guide.cost: Tree, mulch and equipment need a local quote.
guide.scope: North Carolina Extension guidance. Recheck species, season and site rules elsewhere.
guide.suitability: A permitted ground site with room for the mature canopy and roots and someone to provide establishment care.
materials: Site plan and utility-location information
A suitable nursery tree and planting instructions
Shovel, gloves, water source and organic mulch
Plant label and care record
constraints: Confirm owner permission and utility-marking requirements before excavation.
Do not plant under overhead wires or where mature roots/canopy conflict with infrastructure.
Large trees, heavy root balls and work near structures require qualified help.

steps.title: Check the mature tree’s space
instructions: Observe site light, moisture and available root/canopy space. Confirm permission and buried-utility procedures.
Use local guidance to choose a species suited to this actual site, then confirm nursery planting requirements.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the approved site and chosen species requirements.

steps.title: Prepare a correctly sized hole
instructions: Measure the root ball. For the container-grown tree in this guide, dig no deeper than the root ball and two to three times wider.
Find the trunk flare and ask the nursery about circling roots. Stop and get help if the tree is too heavy or awkward to move.
steps.checkpoint: Confirm depth and trunk-flare position before backfilling.

steps.title: Plant, water and mulch
instructions: Position the trunk flare at or slightly above the surrounding ground, backfill with removed soil and water it in.
Add 2 to 3 inches of organic mulch, keeping it at least 6 inches from the trunk. Follow nursery guidance for any support.
steps.checkpoint: Record species, planting date and the actual planted count.

steps.title: Care through establishment
instructions: Check root-ball moisture and adjust watering to actual rain, soil and plant condition rather than a fixed forecast rule.
Keep mulch away from the trunk and record a care check. Ask Extension about problems you cannot identify.
steps.checkpoint: Record survival and the next establishment check.

guide.completion: One permitted tree was planted and its establishment care was recorded.
guide.followup: Continue establishment checks. Planting does not update AQI or a household score.

fit.requires: Keep paths, drains and local fire-clearance areas clear.

guide.title: Make a small winter habitat corner
guide.description: Keep a manageable patch of leaves and stems for seasonal habitat.
guide.purpose: Retain suitable ground and plant cover in a permitted area.
guide.effort: One site check and a seasonal follow-up
guide.cost: Use suitable material already on the site.
guide.scope: US Fish and Wildlife seasonal guidance. Local fire, drainage and property rules take priority.
guide.suitability: A permitted planted corner that can remain clear of paths, drains and required fire-clearance areas.
materials: Small site sketch
Existing suitable leaves and standing plant stems
Gloves and hand tools if needed
A seasonal observation record
constraints: Keep exits, walking routes and drains unobstructed.
Do not retain hazardous standing dead trees or work on trees yourself.
Follow local fire-clearance, pest and property requirements; do not move unknown plant material from another site.

steps.title: Choose a permitted corner clear of hazards
instructions: Confirm permission and a small planted area away from exits and drainage infrastructure.
Check whether local fire-clearance or site-management rules require a different location.
steps.checkpoint: Record the boundary and permission.

steps.title: Retain suitable leaves and stems
instructions: Leave appropriate leaf cover and standing stems in the chosen area rather than clearing everything.
Keep walkways and drains clear. Do not add hazardous snags or move unknown plants into the patch.
steps.checkpoint: Record what was retained and where.

steps.title: Check the patch after weather
instructions: Observe whether leaves are blowing onto paths or blocking drainage and correct those access issues.
Leave resident insects undisturbed. Record visible conditions without guessing species or survival counts.
steps.checkpoint: Keep one factual site check.

steps.title: Plan the seasonal transition
instructions: Use local seasonal guidance before pruning or removing habitat cover.
Consider early and late flowering plants for the next planting season if the site supports them.
steps.checkpoint: Choose one seasonal review and any plant-selection question.

guide.completion: A suitable habitat patch was retained and a seasonal care review was chosen.
guide.followup: Recheck access, drainage and plant care without inventing biodiversity gains.

sources.title: Keep earthworms out of natural environments

fit.requires: Choose and maintain the method that fits your space; a collection program must be verified.

guide.title: Start a manageable compost system
guide.description: Choose a method that fits your space and keep the material stream clean.
guide.purpose: Handle suitable food and garden scraps through a maintained compost method.
guide.effort: Setup and regular care over several months
guide.cost: A bin, bedding or collection service may have a cost. Check the method you choose.
guide.scope: EPA household compost guidance. Collection programs have their own accepted-material rules.
guide.suitability: A permitted backyard bin, a maintainable indoor worm system or a genuinely available collection program.
materials: Chosen method and its accepted-material list
Suitable closed scrap container
Bin, bedding or collection container appropriate to the method
A maintenance record
constraints: Do not put meat, dairy, greasy food, pet waste or treated wood into the backyard method in this guide.
A collection service must confirm accepted materials; a compostable label is not enough.
Do not release compost worms outdoors. Use a suitable species and maintain the selected bin.

steps.title: Choose a method you can maintain
instructions: Read the backyard and worm-bin methods and choose only one that fits your space and care capacity.
If using a collection program instead, verify its actual location, accepted materials and service requirements.
steps.checkpoint: Record the method, permission and responsible person.

steps.title: Set up a clean material stream
instructions: Keep fruit/vegetable scraps in a closed container and retain an accepted-material list near it.

For backyard compost, prepare dry browns and a draining bin area. For indoor worms, use a dark, covered bin with product-specified aeration/drainage, suitable purchased red wigglers and damp, non-glossy paper bedding filling about half the bin.
For a worm bin, let damp bedding drain before adding it, fluff it and keep the bin shaded. Use the source’s measured bin plan with adult tool help if building instead of buying.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the specific container and material rules.

steps.title: Maintain the chosen method
instructions: For a backyard pile, use at least two to three volumes of browns to one of greens, cover scraps and maintain moist-sponge consistency.

For worms, maintain the source’s 59°F to 77°F range where feasible. After they settle for a few days, add a small amount of suitable scraps under 1 to 2 inches of bedding; wait until food is eaten before adding more.
Do not turn or stir a worm bin like a hot compost pile. Mist dry bedding rather than pouring water into it, and use the source’s troubleshooting for odor or feeding problems.
steps.checkpoint: Record your actual maintenance and any odor or moisture adjustment.

steps.title: Review the result honestly
instructions: For backyard compost, wait until the pile is no longer heating and visible scraps have decomposed, then cure for at least four weeks. Do not call dried food scraps finished compost.
For a worm bin, use the source’s harvest method and retain the worms/egg capsules for the maintained bin; do not release them into natural areas.
Record material handled or finished compost only if observed or measured, and choose the next care check.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a real outcome or leave the project ongoing.

guide.completion: The chosen system is operating with correct material rules and ongoing care. Setup is not proof that finished compost exists.
guide.followup: Continue maintenance or a verified collection routine. Do not calculate emissions saved from a checklist.

guide.title: Plan a rain garden before digging
guide.description: Find out whether an observed runoff route has a suitable planting solution.
guide.purpose: Produce an informed site plan, not an unreviewed drainage construction project.
guide.effort: A site observation and local consultation
guide.cost: Planning can use a sketch; design or installation may require a quote.
guide.scope: North Carolina landscape guidance. Local design and drainage requirements remain essential.
guide.suitability: A permitted yard with observed runoff and access to local site/design advice.
materials: Site sketch and observed runoff notes
Foundation, well and septic-system locations if known
Utility-location requirements
A local Extension or stormwater contact
constraints: Do not start excavation until the site and utility requirements are resolved.
The source excludes locations within 10 feet of a foundation or 25 feet of a wellhead or septic drain field.
Do not redirect runoff onto neighboring property or assume a rain garden resolves contamination or flooding.

steps.title: Document actual runoff
instructions: From stable footing, sketch where roof or paved-area runoff goes. Do not go outside in dangerous weather to observe it.
Distinguish an observed route from a guess based on rainfall forecasts.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the date and actual runoff observation.

steps.title: Identify exclusion areas
instructions: Mark structures, wellheads, septic fields, known utilities and access routes on the sketch.
Apply the source’s clearance rules and flag unknown groundwater, soil or utility conditions for qualified review.
steps.checkpoint: Keep exclusions and unresolved site questions.

steps.title: Get a site-specific review
instructions: Ask a local Extension or stormwater resource whether this location and runoff route are suitable.
Request appropriate sizing, soil/infiltration and overflow guidance. Do not let the app invent those dimensions.
steps.checkpoint: Record the contact route and reviewed recommendations or pending questions.

steps.title: Keep a plan or choose another option
instructions: Record the proposed location and next permission/design steps if suitability is established.
If the site is unsuitable or still uncertain, record that result and consider a different stewardship project.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a reviewed plan or an honest decision not to proceed.

guide.completion: A site plan or suitability decision was recorded. This guide does not claim that a rain garden was built.
guide.followup: Only begin a separate installation after design, permissions and maintenance responsibilities are resolved.

Manufacturer installation instructions
Stable support and approved overflow route
Maintenance and non-potable-use label
constraints: Do not drink this water or use it to wash or irrigate edible plants in this guide.
A filled barrel is heavy. Follow qualified installation and product support requirements.
Keep access secured and openings covered/screened; check local rules before modifying a downspout.

steps.title: Confirm permission and ornamental use
instructions: Check local collection rules and owner permission before buying or changing drainage.
Identify only non-edible ornamental plants for this guide. Appearance and smell cannot establish water quality.
steps.checkpoint: Record permission and the intended non-potable use.

steps.title: Resolve stable support and overflow
instructions: Use product installation instructions and qualified help to resolve stable support, secure access and overflow.
Keep runoff away from foundations and neighbors; do not invent a support height or platform design.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the support/overflow instructions and any installer contact.

steps.title: Install and label the system
instructions: Install only after the support and drainage requirements are established.
Keep the lid and screens in place, label the water non-potable and inspect fittings without climbing or entering the barrel.
steps.checkpoint: Record actual installation and the safety check.

steps.title: Maintain and inspect
instructions: Follow the product and local seasonal instructions to clean, drain and inspect the system.
Use collected water only for the ornamental use chosen here and record a care check.
steps.checkpoint: Keep maintenance and any issue requiring help.

guide.completion: A permitted system was installed with a support, overflow, access and maintenance plan.
guide.followup: Review condition and seasonal shutdown. Do not claim a measured water saving without compatible records.

fit.requires: Resolve the actual garden-water source and the watering instructions that apply.

guide.title: Tune your garden watering routine
guide.description: Observe one planting area and keep water on the plants, not the pavement.
guide.purpose: Improve a practical watering routine using actual plant needs and local instructions.
guide.effort: One observation and a follow-up check
guide.cost: Observation requires no new controller. Repairs or equipment need a quote.
guide.scope: EPA water-efficiency guidance. Applicable utility rules and site needs take priority.
guide.suitability: A permitted garden with a known irrigation source and someone able to adjust or report problems.
materials: Plant/site notes
Known water source and current utility instructions
Watering or irrigation instructions
A simple observation record
constraints: Confirm the irrigation source; household drinking-water context is not automatically garden-water context.
Do not set a universal watering amount from outdoor humidity or a single rain forecast.
Electrical, pressurized-system or buried-pipe repairs require qualified help.

steps.title: Resolve the water source and needs
instructions: Record the actual garden-water source or leave it unknown and ask the responsible person.
Use plant instructions and local Extension or utility advice to establish appropriate watering and restrictions.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the source and the site-specific instructions.

steps.title: Observe one watering session
instructions: From stable footing, check whether water lands on pavement, pools or runs off before soaking in.
Record the date, planting area and what you observed. Do not translate runoff into a pollutant measurement.
steps.checkpoint: Keep one actual observation.

steps.title: Make or request a suitable adjustment
instructions: Adjust simple permitted watering placement so it targets the planting area, following the equipment instructions.
Ask the owner or irrigation professional about leaks, pressure or drainage issues rather than attempting unsafe repairs.
steps.checkpoint: Record the adjustment or request actually made.

steps.title: Check the planting response
instructions: Review plant condition and pooling on a later occasion and note rain or weather differences.
Choose a continued care check. Any measured-use comparison must retain matching meters, units and interval lengths.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a factual response and one next check.

guide.completion: A known watering context was checked and an actual suitable adjustment or request was recorded.
guide.followup: Review the routine as plant and seasonal conditions change.

guide.title: Find a hidden household water leak
guide.description: Do a small leak check and keep a clear repair or landlord follow-up.
guide.purpose: Identify a practical water-maintenance question without guessing water loss.
guide.effort: A short check and a repair follow-up
guide.cost: Food coloring or a dye tablet if suitable; repairs require a quote.
guide.suitability: A permitted household check with easy access to fixtures. Renters can report rather than repair.
materials: Clock or timer
Food coloring or a suitable dye tablet
Fixture instructions and a careful way to handle the tank lid
A landlord, owner or plumber contact
constraints: Do not lift a heavy tank lid without suitable help.
Follow fixture instructions and flush after the dye check to avoid staining.
Do not open walls, modify plumbing or attempt electrical/pressurized repairs.

steps.title: Look for actual dripping or running
instructions: Check accessible faucets and fixtures for visible dripping or unexpected running.
Record where and when it occurred. A large bill alone does not identify the cause.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the fixture and observed condition.

steps.title: Do the toilet dye check if suitable
instructions: With help lifting the lid and permission, add a few drops of food coloring or a dye tablet to the tank.
Without flushing, wait 10 minutes and observe the bowl. Flush immediately afterward to avoid staining.
steps.checkpoint: Record whether color appeared, or why the check was not suitable.

steps.title: Arrange the right follow-up
instructions: If the check indicates a leak or the fixture has another problem, inform the owner/landlord or ask a plumber.
Use the exact fixture model and appropriate instructions before considering any permitted simple repair.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the request, provider or repair actually completed.

steps.title: Recheck after a confirmed repair
instructions: Repeat the appropriate observation after the repair and keep its actual result.
Record water usage only from real compatible measurements. Do not calculate saved gallons from a repaired checkbox.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the follow-up result or remaining question.

guide.completion: A suitable check and its real finding were recorded, with a repair or follow-up resolved or still waiting.
guide.followup: Keep the owner/plumber reply and a later leak check if needed.

guide.title: Match your garden question to a soil test
guide.description: Find the right laboratory scope before collecting a sample.
guide.purpose: Resolve whether a garden question needs fertility advice, contaminant testing or qualified site review.
guide.effort: A focused question and laboratory conversation
guide.cost: The selected lab must provide current fees.
guide.scope: North Carolina Extension soil-testing guidance. Exact laboratory scope must be confirmed locally.
guide.suitability: An existing or proposed garden site with a question or an unclear report.
materials: Site label and known soil history
One answerable question
Existing report with its original units and qualifiers if available
Provider-confirmed laboratory instructions
constraints: A routine fertility panel does not certify crop safety or screen every contaminant.
Do not infer contamination from an unknown source, home age or nearby facility.
Obtain the lab’s matrix/analyte/method and collection instructions before sampling.

steps.title: Write the precise soil question
instructions: Separate a plant-nutrient question from a suspected contaminant question.
Keep known soil history and leave unknown supplier, source or test information unresolved.
steps.checkpoint: Record the site and precise question.

steps.title: Review the report’s scope
instructions: Keep the original matrix, analytes, units, dates and qualifiers from any existing report.
Ask about missing units or unclear sample basis instead of converting or treating a censored value as zero.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the actual report fields and uncertainties.

steps.title: Ask a lab or Extension resource
instructions: Ask which service addresses the question, its matrix/analyte/method scope and current fees.
For a complex suspected contaminated site, ask about qualified site assessment rather than an app-generated sampling design.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the response or a pending contact route.

steps.title: Keep instructions and a deliberate next step
instructions: If proceeding, retain the chosen lab’s exact collection, labeling and delivery requirements before collecting.
Continue in Homeguard with the actual test arrangement or record that no appropriate test has yet been selected.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a scoped testing plan or an unresolved question.

guide.completion: The test purpose and appropriate service were clarified, or remaining limitations were documented.
guide.followup: Link the actual report to its garden site without turning it into a crop-safety score.

guide.title: Try a food-waste reduction week
guide.description: Observe what gets discarded, then test one practical kitchen change.
guide.purpose: Reduce avoidable food waste through a small observed routine change.
guide.effort: Short daily observations across a week
guide.cost: Use a paper or app record. No new equipment is required.
guide.scope: EPA household food-waste guidance. Follow food-safety and product storage instructions.
guide.suitability: A kitchen or shared household routine you can influence, without needing a yard.
materials: A simple discarded-food log
Existing pantry/fridge inventory
Shopping and meal plan
Food-storage instructions from the source
constraints: Do not eat food that may be unsafe to avoid recording waste.
Keep required cold storage and product safety instructions.
Only actual observations or measurements can become quantities; inventory presence does not prove waste.

steps.title: Observe what is actually discarded
instructions: For a few days, note the food and reason it was discarded, such as forgotten leftovers or buying more than needed.
Keep this separate from unsafe food that must be discarded and from inedible scraps.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a real baseline observation.

steps.title: Choose one practical change
instructions: Use your observation to select one change, such as checking existing food before shopping or planning a leftovers meal.
Follow the source’s storage instructions; do not invent shelf life or override a recall.
steps.checkpoint: Record the single change you chose.

steps.title: Try the change and record outcomes
instructions: Continue the same simple log while trying your chosen change.
Record food actually used or discarded, not a promised saving from the shopping plan.
steps.checkpoint: Keep comparable observations and relevant changes in household routine.

steps.title: Review what is worth keeping
instructions: Compare your observations and identify whether the change was practical. A week cannot establish a long-term emissions effect.
For unavoidable scraps, consider an appropriate maintained compost or confirmed collection option.
steps.checkpoint: Keep one useful routine or an honest decision to try something else.

guide.completion: One routine change was tried and its observed outcome recorded.
guide.followup: Keep the useful routine or repeat a simple observation without a streak or invented impact total.

guide.title: Understand a damp room
guide.description: Keep actual indoor observations and a focused owner or maintenance follow-up.
guide.purpose: Clarify a moisture source without diagnosing indoor mold from an outdoor forecast.
guide.effort: One indoor check and a follow-up
guide.cost: A humidity meter can be borrowed or priced locally; professional help may cost.
guide.scope: EPA home-moisture guidance. This is an observation project, not remediation instructions.
guide.suitability: An easily accessible room with condensation, a leak question or a chosen indoor humidity check.
materials: Room label and actual observation date
Optional indoor humidity meter and its instructions
A leak/condensation record
Owner, landlord or qualified maintenance contact
constraints: Outdoor humidity and rain estimates do not establish indoor humidity or detected mold.
Do not disturb suspected contaminated material, open walls or enter unsafe damp areas.
Report leaks and significant moisture problems to the responsible owner or qualified resource.

steps.title: Record what you can actually observe
instructions: From stable footing, record condensation, a visible leak or a damp area and its actual date.
Do not label a visual observation as a contaminant measurement or assign a mold concentration.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the factual room observation.

steps.title: Keep indoor readings separate
instructions: If using a humidity meter, follow its instructions and record the actual number, original unit, room and time.
Compare readings only in their actual indoor context. The outdoor forecast is a different source.
steps.checkpoint: Keep an actual indoor reading or explicitly no measurement.

steps.title: Address the source through the right person
instructions: Report plumbing leaks or recurring moisture to the owner/landlord or a qualified maintenance resource.
Follow the existing ventilation and equipment instructions. This guide does not prescribe removing contaminated material.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the request or permitted action actually taken.

steps.title: Review after the response
instructions: Keep the repair/response and recheck the room from stable footing.
Record whether the observed issue remains, without treating a checklist as proof of a health improvement.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the actual follow-up and unresolved limits.

guide.completion: A factual indoor record and an appropriate follow-up were kept.
guide.followup: Continue the chosen maintenance or landlord conversation in Homeguard.

guide.title: Check your drinking-water filter plan
guide.description: Match the exact product claim and instructions to the question you want answered.
guide.purpose: Review a real filter’s scope and maintenance without assuming a generic filter removes every contaminant.
guide.effort: Product/source review and a care follow-up
guide.cost: Check actual product, replacement and service prices.
guide.scope: EPA PFAS-filter guidance. Certification scope and current product instructions must be checked.
guide.suitability: A household that has or is considering an appropriate drinking-water filter. A utility sample is not a tap test.
materials: Exact filter model and product instructions
The specific contaminant question
Certification listing and its precise reduction claim
A manufacturer-supported maintenance plan
constraints: Do not infer certification or effectiveness from a generic filter record.
Follow the exact product’s installation and maintenance requirements; use qualified help where needed.
A utility sample or completed replacement does not establish the household’s current tap-water result.

steps.title: Identify the exact question and product
instructions: Keep the actual filter model or explicitly record that it is unknown.
Name the contaminant question and retain the scope/date of any public water sample separately.
steps.checkpoint: Record model and question without guessing.

steps.title: Review the precise certification claim
instructions: Use the official certification/product route linked by the source to check the exact model’s reduction claims.
Keep what the claim covers and does not cover. Ask the water provider or qualified resource about unresolved suitability.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the actual certification scope or an unresolved lookup.

steps.title: Choose a supported maintenance routine
instructions: Read the exact product’s cartridge and care instructions rather than inventing a monthly schedule.
Only add a Homeguard routine after you deliberately choose its instructions and date.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the source-backed routine or the missing instruction question.

steps.title: Record actual care and a review
instructions: Record service or replacement only when it actually happens, retaining its date and instructions.
If a tap-water answer is needed, ask a certified lab for the appropriate testing method rather than assuming the care result.
steps.checkpoint: Keep actual care or a deliberate testing follow-up.

guide.completion: The product scope and care requirements were clarified or their remaining uncertainty recorded.
guide.followup: Continue the exact product routine or laboratory question in Homeguard.

DIY air-cleaner designs and equipment safety

fit.requires: Use the exact reviewed electrical and equipment requirements. No smoke or indoor condition is inferred.

guide.title: Prepare a particle-filtration setup
guide.description: Review a suitable indoor cleaner or the source’s supervised DIY alternative.
guide.purpose: Prepare equipment for particle filtration without claiming an indoor-air measurement or personal protection guarantee.
guide.effort: Equipment review and a supervised setup
guide.cost: Price an appropriate commercial cleaner or exact DIY materials locally.
guide.scope: EPA wildfire-particle guidance. AQI alone does not establish smoke or indoor particle concentration.
guide.suitability: A suitable indoor space, permission and compatible equipment. The DIY build needs an adult and the source’s exact safety requirements.
materials: Appropriate commercial equipment instructions, or the reviewed DIY design
For the basic DIY: matching 20-inch fan and MERV 13 filter
Only a 2012-or-newer fan with UL/ETL safety marking for the DIY method
Suitable clamps, tape or bungee cords and source safety instructions
constraints: Do not infer smoke, indoor air quality or health benefit from AQI alone.
Follow source and manufacturer electrical/fire safety instructions; no altered wiring or unverified old fan.
Particle filtration is not a radon, gas or ventilation solution.

steps.title: Choose an equipment path
instructions: Review a commercial air cleaner suitable for the room or the source’s DIY method as a temporary alternative.
Confirm permission and electrical safety. Keep an outdoor reading separate from unknown indoor conditions.
steps.checkpoint: Keep the chosen design and its safety requirements.

steps.title: Check exact materials and instructions
instructions: For the basic DIY, use a matching fan and MERV 13 filter, with a 2012-or-newer UL/ETL-marked fan.
Read the complete source’s safety FAQ and manufacturer instructions before assembly; do not assume every fan/filter configuration was tested.
steps.checkpoint: Record the actual equipment and safety checks.

steps.title: Set up only as instructed
instructions: For the reviewed basic DIY, secure the filter to the back of the fan and align its airflow arrow with fan airflow.
Follow instructions for secure placement, operation and any supervision. Do not modify wiring, obstruct required clearances or use damaged equipment.
steps.checkpoint: Record the supervised setup or why it could not proceed.

steps.title: Keep a real care record
instructions: Follow instructions to check and replace dirty filters and retain the actual dates.
Record equipment care, not an invented reduction in indoor particles or symptoms.
steps.checkpoint: Keep a care instruction and chosen follow-up.

guide.completion: Appropriate equipment was reviewed and set up following its safety instructions, or the remaining equipment/safety question was recorded.
guide.followup: Keep manufacturer-supported care. An actual indoor measurement requires its own valid instrument and protocol.
